entries.title: First day of practice: Maine South holds on as one of the few public-school powers in high school football
entries.summary: <p>Private schools have won the past four Class 8A football state championships and dominated most of the larger classes overall. The talent gap between public and private schools is even more stark this season. Catholic League teams will make up the majority of the preseason Super 25.</p><p>There are many factors for the rise of the Catholic powers. One is coaching. Private schools are attracting the best young coaches. The few public schools managing to maintain relevance are coached by a handful of elite veteran coaches.</p><p>Dave Inserra, now in his 26th season, is one of those. He’s won four state championships and guided his team to eight title games.</p><p>But most of the successful public-school coaches are nearing the end of their careers. Inserra reflected on the current situation Wednesday, the first day of football practice across the state.</p><p>“How many years do we have left?” Inserra said. “And then what happens?</p><p>“My biggest concern is the [IHSA’s rule allowing kids to attend private schools within a] 30-mile radius. Why does anyone have to travel 30 miles to go to school? A 15-mile radius I could understand.”</p><p>Inserra has built something special in Park Ridge. Strong feeder programs and a community rabid about high school football has kept the Hawks competitive.</p><p>This year’s team is led by a trio of major college recruits. Quarterback Jameson Purcell, an Indiana recruit, is a three-year starter and one of the state’s elite talents. He threw for more than 3,000 yards and 41 TDs last season.</p><p>“For me this season is about putting all the pieces together and being a complete player,” Purcell said. "That starts with being the best leader I can, especially with a little bit of a younger team this year.”</p><p>Most of Maine South’s offensive line returns, led by Toledo recruit Vuk Strbac (6-5, 275 pounds) and Inserra has confidence in receivers Keaton Vitel and Nick McCarthy.</p><p>“We put a lot on [Purcell’s] shoulders, and he has accepted that,” Inserra said. “Be he doesn’t have to do everything.”</p><p>Senior linebacker Matthew Schlenhardt will also play running back this season. The Syracuse recruit is the only starter back on the defense.</p><p>“There is definitely some work to do,” Schlenhardt said. “A lot of guys have the skill it is just about knowing the playbook and doing everything right. If you do everything right, it is going to work. So that is the big thing right now.”</p><p>Maine South finished 10-2 last season and lost a close game to Hersey in the 8A quarterfinals.</p><p>“That was kind of an upset and it has given us a different mentality this year,” Strbac said. “We are bringing it.”</p><p>Vitel also plays cornerback and will team with safety Hugh Stewart and linemen Mark Orszula and Aidan Connolly to lead the Hawks’ inexperienced defense.</p><p>Football started a week earlier this season, and the IHSA has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2025/12/16/ihsa-expanded-football-playoffs-illinois" >expanded the playoffs by 128 teams</a>. It will likely take just three or four wins to make the playoffs now, instead of five wins.</p><p>“I’m not happy with the expansion,” Inserra said. “It was a pretty good format before. Not perfect. But the change favors private schools. A 3-6 private school is going to walk into the playoffs and be in the quarterfinals.”</p><p>Maine South has dominated the CSL South for Inserra’s entire tenure. Most years, many of the Hawks’ late-season opponents are already eliminated from the playoffs, with their season essentially pointless. The expansion changes that.</p><p>“That’s the one positive thing,” Inserra said. “You start the season1-3 and the kids start to think things are useless. This gives them some life. I get that. I haven’t faced that so I can’t say I understand it, but I get that part.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-170000" name="html-embed-module-170000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports/video/7670562132374719775" data-video-id="7670562132374719775" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports?refer=embed">@michaelsobriensports</a> Football season begins! Maine South LB Matthew Schlenhardt, a Syracuse recruit, looks ahead to the Hawks’ season. <a title="ihsa" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/ihsa?refer=embed">#ihsa</a> <a title="football" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/football?refer=embed">#football</a> <a title="mainesouth" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/mainesouth?refer=embed">#mainesouth</a> <a title="syracuse" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/syracuse?refer=embed">#syracuse</a> <a title="parkridge" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/parkridge?refer=embed">#parkridge</a> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-7670562115765242654?refer=embed">♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: What to know about diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>Illinois has confirmed 995 confirmed and probable cases of the diarrhea-causing illness cyclosporiasis, the state’s public health department confirmed Tuesday.</p><p>Cyclosporiasis is not considered deadly and is more of an inconvenience that in rare cases could have complications, said Dr. Emily Landon, an infectious diseases specialist at University of Chicago Medicine. In Illinois, 58 people have been hospitalized, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. Most of the people in Illinois who have contracted the illness had traveled recently — 193 people internationally and 631<b> </b>domestically. It’s unclear if the other 171 traveled.</p><p>Higher numbers of cyclosporiasis are typically reported in the summer, but this year has seen an especially high number, health officials said.</p><p>The increase in Illinois is part of a larger number of cases in several states. In Michigan, which has been at the center of an outbreak nationally, two people with significant health conditions died, health officials announced on Aug. 3, saying that cyclosporiasis and dehydration contributed to the deaths. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services is reporting <a class="Link" href="https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/keep-mi-healthy/infectious-diseases/infectious-disease-outbreaks" target="_blank" >12,218 cases</a> as of Wednesday. Across the country, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports just 1,947 cases in nine states, which is far less than Michigan alone. Those cases were linked to eating at Taco Bell, according to the CDC and the FDA. <b></b></p><p>Here's what you need to know about cyclosporiasis in Illinois.</p><h3><b>What is cyclosporiasis?</b></h3><p>Pronounced sigh-klo-spore-EYE-uh-sis, cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora. Infection often comes after eating fresh fruits and vegetables and can lead to watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, gas and nausea.</p><p>The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water. </p><h3><b>What is causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois?</b></h3><p>No definitive source has been identified for the Illinois cases, but public health officials have been investigating a link to iceberg lettuce. Taylor Fresh Foods, a California-based farm and food company, on July 17 voluntarily recalled iceberg salad and shredded lettuce products distributed in 27 states, including Illinois. In other states, Marketside-brand iceberg products sold at select Walmart stores were also recalled. </p><p>The FDA on July 19 said that initial testing for cyclospora in a sample of lettuce from Taylor Farms was a false positive. The products in question from Taylor Farms were grown in the Mexican state of Guanajuato. The FDA encourages the public to avoid eating any products recalled by Taylor Farms, and the CDC recommends that anyone who purchased the recalled lettuce should throw it out.</p><p>The voluntary recall came after the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/index.html" target="_blank" >CDC</a> identified shredded lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia as a source of widespread outbreaks in those states. Taco Bell removed the affected lettuce from its supply chain across the country and planned to replace it in select states, the company previously said. Taylor Farms supplied lettuce to Taco Bell, The New York Times reported.</p><p>The CDC is also investigating other cases of cyclosporiasis that are not connected to the national outbreak.</p><p>Past outbreaks have been linked to imported fresh produce, like bagged salad kits and berries, according to IDPH. Cyclosporiasis is not transmitted from person to person, Landon said. Even if a person becomes sick, people don’t usually contaminate objects in their house enough to spread it to someone else.</p><h3><b>How long does it take to recover?</b></h3><p>People should talk to their doctor about getting tested if they have symptoms, so health officials can continue to track the outbreak, said Gwen Biggerstaff, the CDC’s deputy director of foodborne, waterborne and environmental diseases.</p><p>Most people who contract the illness recover in one to two weeks, according to the CDC. Many can recover with rest and plenty of fluids, but some may need antibiotics.</p><p>People can experience bloating, gas and dehydration but rarely have more complications.</p><p>“The problem with this disease is it can be kind of persistent,” Landon said. “And you can feel pretty sick, and then you can be starting to get better, and then the diarrhea can come back again.” </p><h3><b>Should I stop eating fresh fruits and vegetables? </b></h3><p>If a person is immunocompromised or has an underlying medical condition, they should take more precautions, Landon said. That’s especially true, for example, for those undergoing surgery soon or cancer treatments.</p><p>Everyone can follow typical food safety guidelines like washing hands and thoroughly washing and scrubbing fresh produce. Illinois health officials also suggest:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-b5494250-808c-11f1-a776-3b92d1e3bbf6"><li>Incorporating more fruits and vegetables with peels or outer layers</li><li>Eating canned fruits and vegetables</li><li>Keeping produce separate from raw meat and seafood</li><li>Refrigerating cut, peeled, or cooked fruits and vegetables within two hours</li><li>Refrigerating perishable produce.</li><li>Cooking vegetables to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit </li></ul><h3><b>Is it safer to buy produce from my local Illinois farmers market? </b></h3><p>Fruits and vegetables coming from a smaller, local producer are likely to have less of a risk for contamination than food from massive manufacturers, Landon said. That’s especially true if an outbreak is centered on a certain product, but officials this time around don’t know if that’s the case.</p><p>So you shouldn’t assume there’s zero risk in buying from a local vendor because any farm can become contaminated, especially because of the current weather, Landon said.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><h3><b>How is Illinois tracking the cases?</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health is working with local health officials to collect data on the cases. They are also working with the CDC to investigate a potential source of the illness.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Public Health has not identified the source of local cases. One individual had eaten at Taco Bell but had also traveled to one of the states that is part of the larger outbreak. The department is seeing an increase in cases among Latinos who had not recently traveled internationally.</p><p>The number of cases locally and across the country could be higher, Landon said. That’s because testing for cyclosporiasis is expensive, and some insurance may not cover it. But as cases of cyclosporiasis are more in the news, doctors will likely start testing more patients or prescribe antibiotics to treat it if someone has symptoms.</p><p>If a person is confirmed to have cyclosporiasis, Landon said it’s important to cooperate with the local health department to detail everything they ate so officials can pinpoint the outbreak source.</p><h3><b>Are federal cuts affecting the outbreak? </b></h3><p>Last summer, the federal government scaled back a program known as the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network that monitored foodborne illnesses, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/cdc-quietly-scaled-back-surveillance-program-foodborne-illnesses-rcna227089?link_source=ta_bluesky_link&taid=68add0b9b2316600014ce6de&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_medium=social&utm_source=bluesky" target="_blank" ><u>NBC News previously reported</u></a>. As part of the changes, reporting for cyclospora parasites became optional in 2025, according to the program’s website. The government had previously collected that data since 1997.</p><p>The scaled-back federal program worked with the FDA to proactively test certain foods to check if recalls were necessary, Landon said.</p><p>It’s hard to assess how much changes on the federal level are playing a role in the current outbreaks, Landon said. But it’s something health officials across the country should consider.</p><p>“It’s a combination of the nature of the illness, the fact that it’s happening at a time when there’s other sporadic cases, and then the lack of infrastructure and resources available for testing does matter,” Landon said, summing up the factors driving the outbreak. <br></p>

entries.title: Intruso deja grafiti racista en casa de Brighton Park; la policía lo investiga como posible crimen de odio
entries.summary: <p>La policía investiga un delito de odio después de que una casa en Brighton Park fue vandalizada el lunes.</p><p>Los agentes fueron llamados alrededor de las 9 a.m. después de que el propietario llegara a la casa que está renovando en el lado suroeste. En el interior, había encontrado grafiti racista, según un informe policial obtenido por el Sun-Times. </p><p>Alguien había escrito "F- - - China" con pintura negra en una pared, según el informe.</p><p>El propietario es un hombre de origen asiático.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9d0000" name="module-9d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>También había otros daños en el interior. El propietario dijo a la policía que los intrusos habían dañado tres paneles eléctricos y retirado tuberías de cobre. entries.title: Padres y maestros intentan rescatar libros que aparecieron en contenedores afuera de las escuelas Acero
entries.summary: <p>Sarah Parchem se quedó sin aliento cuando el domingo se topó con una publicación en Facebook que mostraba un contenedor lleno de libros y útiles escolares fuera de la Escuela Primaria Fuentes, en el vecindario de Avondale.</p><p>Como madre de un niño que va a empezar el kínder y que valora la lectura, Parchem dijo que la foto casi la hizo llorar. Pero también vio una oportunidad. Se subió a su auto y pasó dos horas hurgando en el contenedor esa mañana en busca de cualquier cosa que pudiera rescatar.</p><p>No estuvo sola. Durante días, padres, docentes y miembros de la comunidad buscaron en el contenedor frente a Fuentes cualquier cosa útil. Un contenedor con contenido similar se vio frente a la Escuela Primaria Santiago, en el vecindario de Ukrainian Village.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module entries.title: 'Stone-cold killer' linked to slayings of 2 teen girlfriends was caught on jailhouse wire: prosecutors
entries.summary: <p>Paranoid his girlfriend was betraying him to a rival gang, Anthony Nunnally allegedly shot and killed her in an East Side alley last October, prosecutors said in court Wednesday.</p><p>Just over a year before that, he allegedly killed another girlfriend in a different East Side alley in September 2024, shooting her several times. </p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/04/anthony-nunnally-gabriella-arellano-sierra-evans" target="_blank" >21-year-old was charged this week </a>with two counts of first-degree murder for their deaths. On Wednesday afternoon, Cook County Circuit Court Judge Deidre Dyer ordered him detained until trial.</p><p>Nunnally was already in Cook County jail for an unrelated carjacking charge. He allegedly tried to steal the car of a friend from grade school last October, around the time of the second killing, Cook County prosecutors said in court Wednesday. </p><p>At one point during his incarceration, his cellmate was a former member of the Latin Kings, the Chicago street gang to which Nunnally also allegedly belongs. The cellmate, wearing a wire, got Nunnally talking about the October 2025 murder, Cook County Assistant State's Attorney Mike Pekara said in court. </p><p>Unaware he was being recorded, Nunnally told his cellmate that he was paranoid his 17-year-old girlfriend, Gabriella Arellano, was going to "backdoor him," slang for betraying him to a rival gang. </p><p>When the cellmate asked if he felt any remorse for killing her, Nunnally allegedly said: "When some b - - - - backdoor you, you gotta do what you gotta do," according to Pekara. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/10/26/woman-shot-east-side" target="_blank" >Arellano was found shot once in the head</a> in an alley in the 11000 block of South Mackinaw Avenue on Oct. 26, 2025. Prosecutors said Wednesday that a nearby Ring camera captured the sound of the gunshot and then Nunnally and an unknown person running from the area. Another surveillance camera showed Nunnally, Arellano and the unknown person in the area before the girl was killed. </p><h3>2024 murder</h3><p>About a year earlier, on Sept. 28, 2024, 19-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/09/28/woman-found-shot-to-death-on-far-south-side" target="_blank" >Sierra Evans was found shot</a> several times in the 9500 block of South Avenue N. Evans and Nunnally had been dating for about a month at the time she was killed, Pekara said. </p><p>The night she died, Evans, Nunnally and two other people were drinking and hanging out in a basement, Pekara said. At one point in the night, Nunnally allegedly got angry with Evans and choked and pinned her against a wall. He also punched a hole in the wall of the basement, at which point he was kicked out of the house, Pekara said. </p><p>Later, he called the two people and said he was in an Uber on his way back to the house, Pekara said. Minutes later, they heard several gunshots. Nunnally came running into the basement, holding a gun. He said he just killed someone and then flashed a gang sign. He did not say he killed Evans, Pekara said. </p><p>Evans was found the next day in a nearby alley with 18 shell casings next to her body. </p><p>About seven months later, Nunnally was allegedly threatening to hurt a new girlfriend. He pulled up a TV news clip of a memorial service for a Evans and told the new girlfriend he was going to do the same thing to her that he did to Evans, according to Pekara. </p><p>Scott Kozicki, the Cook County public defender representing Nunnally, said in court that prosecutors didn't have enough evidence proving Nunnally shot both girls. </p><p>In the 2024 slaying, Kozicki said there was no evidence that the gun Nunnally came into the basement with matched the shell casings found at the crime scene. He also questioned the ability of the Ring camera to pick up the sound of a gunshot from the 2025 murder. </p><p>As for the confession to the Chicago street gang member, Kozicki said it was "really shaky, problematic entrapment." He added that Nunnally's cellmate had a great motive to sell him out. </p><p>"These are a lot of scary stories, but being near gunshots does not mean you participated in a shooting," Kozicki said. </p><p>Pekara pushed back against that claim. </p><p>Nunnally "was the person last seen with each of these young women before they died. He was seen with a gun seconds after the first murder. In the second murder, the Ring camera got the sound of a gunshot and saw [Nunnally] running away," Pekara said. </p><p>"He is a stone-cold killer," Pekara added. "This is not a scary story, it’s a fact."</p>

entries.title: Pritzker asks oil CEOs to return Iran war windfall profits to Illinois consumers: 'You owe it to the people'
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker on Wednesday penned letters to the U.S. CEOs of seven major oil companies, accusing them of "profiteering" from the war in Iran and imploring them to return windfall profits to Illinois consumers, among other demands.</p><p>It's a rare agreement between the Democratic governor and President Donald Trump, who on Monday railed against Chevron and Exxon Mobil for high profits amid the Iran war and said they should "give some of that back to the public."</p><p>"Under the guise of supply disruptions from war in the Middle East, your companies are collecting windfall profits from the hardworking families and businesses in Illinois," <a class="Link" href="https://cms.chicago.suntimes.com/cms/content/edit.jsp?id=0000019f-d309-dc99-abff-df9b8d6f0000&typeId=8195a523-335e-3fbb-a4c1-12dbad30b87e" target="_blank" >Pritzker writes in the letter</a> to the CEOs of Shell, Exxon Mobil Corp., Chevron Corp., Continental Resources Inc., bp America, ConocoPhillips and Occidental Petroleum Corp. "That’s the very definition of profiteering, and you owe it to the people of my state and the nation to disgorge those excess profits and provide meaningful price relief to consumers."</p><p>American oil and gas companies are making massive profits while fighting between the U.S. and Iran hinders petroleum shipments. That has led to consumers worldwide paying more for fuel. The conflict has halted most shipping through of Strait of Hormuz, which serves as a delivery route for a large portion of the world's oil and natural gas supply. </p><p>Trump has criticized oil companies' stark profits, writing in June on social media that he wanted the Justice Department to investigate whether "customers are being 'gouged.'" Trump reiterated that claim in the Oval Office Monday, saying he's not happy with the profits reported by Chevron and Exxon Mobil, even though the higher margins reflected energy prices that increased after Trump launched the war, the Associated Press reported. </p><p>“They made too much money, too much money, “ Trump said. “They ought to give some of that back to the public, and they better cut the retail price.”</p><p>Oil companies don't set the price at the pump, but gas station operators have to raise prices when the cost of oil surges, as it has during the Iran war. </p><p>Pritzker's letter to the CEOs says their businesses are profiting "while families across my state and the nation face sharply higher prices at the pump." Since the war began, the price of regular gasoline in Illinois has risen by more than $1.30 per gallon, averaging $4.34 per gallon statewide and costing residents an additional $2 billion so far, the governor wrote. </p><p>The governor wants CEOs to state whether their company is preparing to return any portion of profits to Illinois consumers via price reductions, direct refunds or other means. He also asks them to provide refining margins and wholesale pricing decisions, as well as detailed information about their refinery and operational decisions that affected the volume of gasoline and diesel fuel available to consumers. Pritzker also is seeking information about executive compensation.</p><p>"Illinoisans have a right to know how your companies are profiting from this conflict, how much of those outsized profits Illinois families are being made to pay, and what steps you will now take to provide them with relief at the pump," Pritzker writes.</p><p>The governor is asking for a response from the CEOs by Aug. 21. <br></p>

entries.title: 'Not OK for us': Bears' offense urgently needs to get back on track as sloppy mistakes resurface
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> have seen worse — way worse — from their offense than this, so it’s not cause for alarm. But it is mildly concerning that quarterback Caleb Williams and his group backslid after a strong start to training camp.</p><p>Ever since they started practicing in pads Monday, the offense hasn’t quite looked right, and while some of that is bound to happen throughout the marathon of camp, the pre-snap hiccups are something the Bears thought they’d buried last season.</p><p>The upside is that, as usual, coach Ben Johnson’s staff isn’t sugarcoating or spinning it. The first step toward fixing a problem is being honest about where it stands, and these coaches don’t have any hesitation to call it out.</p><p>“We've taken a step back, honestly, in our pre-snap communication,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said before practice Wednesday morning. “A lot of times just not being on the same page, not seeing something the same way, not communicating... It can expose you if you're not ready.”</p><p>Taylor mentioned snags in calling the play in the huddle, breaking the huddle and being disciplined at the line of scrimmage, where Johnson uses many shifts and motions that can lead to false starts or delay-of-game penalties if the offense isn’t sharp.</p><p>All of that was hammered to offensive players in a meeting Tuesday and the evening walk-through. Wednesday wasn’t really the day to show they’d fixed those issues since the team held a very short and light practice without pads, but the Bears will be full-go Thursday morning, and that will reveal a lot about the offense’s ability to regroup.</p><p>None of it has been as bad as it was last August, when the Bears embarrassed themselves at the Family Fest practice at Soldier Field. That was their 10th practice of camp, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/03/bears-coach-ben-johnson-sends-qb-caleb-williams-offense-stern-message-about-sloppy-mistakes" >it was such a disaster offensively that Johnson fired a warning shot</a> to the team: “If it continues like that, we’re not going to win many games.”</p><p>It did, in fact, continue like that for quite a while. The Bears closed the preseason with an equally discouraging performance against the Chiefs, rife with errors and sloppiness, then sputtered to an 0-2 start in the regular season.</p><p>The Bears committed the fourth-most false starts (33) and illegal-formation penalties (five) last season, plus five delay-of-game penalties, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nflpenalties.com/" target="_blank" >NFLPenalties.com</a>. Those do more damage than just a handful of yards. They can be drive wreckers by putting the team in second- or third-and-long.</p><p>Throughout training camp last year, Johnson was constantly on Williams about being too slow to get out of the huddle and not keeping the group in sync at the line of scrimmage. They’re much more on the same page now, but there have still been some slipups this week. And this was one element that should’ve looked good from the jump.</p><p>“He has the ability to elevate his play,” Taylor said of Williams. “We need just the consistency down in, down out, the communication in the huddle, out of the huddle, at the line. That’s something that will always be a continued process for Caleb.”</p><p>Johnson said this week there have been “way too many mistakes” and “little things like that start to accumulate,” but was evenhanded in his overall assessment that an increase in missteps was “probably normal with the volume [of plays] continuing to increase, yet it's not OK for us and we're going to nip that in the bud.”</p><p>The Bears still have more than a month to work out these glitches before their season opener at the Panthers, but they aren’t going to get to the more advanced concepts of Johnson’s offense if they’re still stumbling. And while he’s been measured and patience in his reactions so far, he’ll have no reservations about getting a lot louder if necessary.</p>

entries.title: Conductor que iba en sentido contrario en expressway intentaba 'asustar' a mujer que suplicaba por su vida
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre de Aurora permanecía el martes bajo custodia, un día después de que los fiscales afirmaran que manejó en sentido contrario por la autopista Dan Ryan para "asustar" a una mujer que suplicaba por su vida momentos antes de morir a causa de un choque en el que estuvieron involucrados cinco vehículos.</p><p>Juan Ruiz Huerta, de 29 años de edad, fue acusado de asesinato en primer grado, secuestro, privación ilegal de la libertad y agresión agravada <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/31/dan-ryan-crash" target="_blank" >relacionada con el choque del viernes por la noche</a> que mató a la residente de Chicago, Victory A. Swanigan, de 28 años, y dejó a otro conductor gravemente herido.</p><p>Un juez del Condado de Cook ordenó que Ruiz Huerta permaneciera bajo custodia durante una audiencia el lunes en la Corte Penal Leighton. Debe regresar a la corte el 19 de agosto.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1e0000" name="module-1e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los fiscales dijeron durante la audiencia que Ruiz Huerta la había estado pretendiendo románticamente durante meses y que la recogió después de una cita en el salón de belleza que él pagó, cuando se enojó con ella por el "estado de su relación".</p><p>Poco después de las 5:30 p.m. del viernes, Ruiz Huerta ingresó a la Interestatal 94 y arrebasó a vehículos que se desplazaban lentamente y a luces policiales al norte de 31st Street, donde Swanigan gritó pidiendo ayuda, dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>Luego Ruiz Huerta dio una vuelta en U y empezó a conducir a alta velocidad hacia el sur por los carriles de sentido norte de la I-94, mientras la amiga de Swanigan pudo escucharse a sí misma suplicándole que redujera la velocidad, según los fiscales.</p><p>Swanigan le dijo a Ruiz Huerta que tenía "tres hijos a los que quería volver a ver" mientras él seguía acelerando, según dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>Un video de vigilancia de la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA) en 47th Street captó a Ruiz Huerta moviéndose a través de varios carriles a alta velocidad y zigzagueando entre numerosos autos y camiones que circulaban en la dirección correcta, antes de chocar frontalmente con otro automóvil que iba hacia el norte por los carriles exprés y provocar que el vehículo de Ruiz Huerta volcara sobre el separador de concreto y cayera a los carriles locales, según documentos de la corte.</p><p>Los fiscales señalaron que el otro conductor en el choque —que sufrió múltiples fracturas de costillas, una laceración en el hígado y otras lesiones— dijo a los investigadores que intentó cambiar de carril para evitar el choque cuando Ruiz Huerta también cambió de carril.</p><p>El informe de una orden de registro ejecutada en la caja negra del Mazda CX-5 2013 de Ruiz-Huerta mostró que viajaba a 86 millas por hora cinco segundos antes del choque y que al momento del impacto, iba a 78 millas por hora sin que hubiera presión en el freno y con el acelerador presionado al 25%, dijeron las autoridades.</p><p>Swanigan, quien residía en la cuadra 8800 al sur de Normal Avenue en el vecindario de Auburn Gresham, fue declarada muerta en la escena, según la Policía Estatal de Illinois y la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Ruiz Huerta supuestamente les dijo a los agentes que, una vez que supo que Swanigan estaba aterrorizada, él la "puso en peligro para obtener una respuesta de ella" sobre el estado de su relación.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: 'Fail Mary' in mind, Bears CB Tyrique Stevenson still seeking consistency
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/05/bears-lb-t-j-edwards-returns-to-practice-after-missing-first-week-with-calf-injury" target="_blank" >Tyrique Stevenson</a> mentions the “Fail Mary” before you have a chance to.</p><p>One mistake, he said, can get you cast aside by the rest of the NFL. He’s lived it.</p><p>“One play could just … As far as injury, as far as mistakes, as far as anything, this league will forget about you in a heartbeat,” he told the Sun-Times earlier this week. “For me, it’s just constantly sitting on my brain every time I touch the field — ‘Just go out there and lay it on the line and stay focused.’</p><p>“I think for that, that’s how I look at it, just an internal motivation. Every play matters. <i>Every play matters</i>.”</p><p>That’s especially true for Stevenson, whether it’s a training camp snap or the last throw of a 2024 loss against the Commanders. That misplay — Stevenson had his back to the ball, jawing at fans, before misplaying Jayden Daniels’ 52-yard game-winning heave — will follow Stevenson for the rest of his career. His goal is to make it feel, eventually, like more of a footnote.</p><p>“From the Hail Mary, my mindset is, go out here every play and show who you can be, and dominate,” he said, “and everything will fall in line.”</p><p>He knows the stakes in Year 4. So do the Bears.</p><p>Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen can put on tape from Stevenson last year that was astoundingly good — and then watch lapses that were maddening. Coaches spent the offseason urging Stevenson to become the steady presence the defense sorely needs.</p><p>“Tyrique needs to be more consistent,” Allen said.</p><p>That goes beyond the practice field, coach Ben Johnson said. He’s seen growth in Stevenson since the end of last season, when he took a backseat to the team’s two starting outside cornerbacks.</p><p>“It’s really the focus level from being in the building, paying attention in meetings and continuing to apply that on the field throughout a two-plus hour practice,” Johnson said. “So I think we’ve seen strides there. It’s certainly improving … He knows it. So we’re pretty happy with where he’s at.”</p><p>Stevenson has been working at it. Stability in his personal life — he got engaged July 4 — has allowed him to focus his attention on his tasks inside Halas Hall.</p><p>“You have everything on the outside complete,” he said, “so let’s turn around and go be an all-pro.”</p><p>Despite posting the best Pro Football Focus grades of any of his three seasons, Stevenson’s playing time dwindled last season. Counting the playoffs, Stevenson didn’t start five out of the 15 games in which he was healthy. In his first two seasons, he started all but two of 32 — and one was the oh-so-brief benching after the “Fail Mary.” Stevenson played just 18 defensive snaps in Week 17 and none in Week 18. He appeared in 14 snaps in the Bears’ playoff win against the Packers and 18 in their loss to the Rams.</p><p>For Stevenson, this season is the last chance for him to prove that he’s a reliable starter before he becomes a free agent in March. He’s run with the starters every day during training camp, with a banged-up Terell Smith and fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad II playing behind him.</p><p>During camp practices, Stevenson is being tested by receiver Luther Burden, who’s earned praise from almost everyone inside Halas Hall this offseason, and held his own. Tuesday, he intercepted Caleb Williams after a miscommunication between the quarterback and tight end Colston Loveland.</p><p>“He's been challenging us,” Burden said. “Making plays out there.”</p><p>He’ll be targeted when games begin, too — teams will avoid throwing toward two-time Pro Bowl cornerback Jaylon Johnson, who’s recovered from last year’s groin surgery.</p><p>Stevenson has the physical skills to be dominant — that’s been apparent since the team made him the 56<sup>th</sup> pick in 2023. When he makes mistakes, he said, they’re rooted in subtleties of his technique. That comes down to focus.</p><p>“It’s one of the things I do daily to keep my mind coming back to the main point — focus and lock in and make the play you know you can make,” he said. “The frustrating part is, ‘We’ve seen you make the plays and we’ve seen you make them multiple times. So why not this time?’”</p><p>What the future holds, he’s not sure. Stevenson tries not to think about free agency. He knows it won’t help his mindset.</p><p>“I don’t want to create an extra block of worry or anxiety that’s not needed,” he said.</p><p>The Bears need him more than ever. They let cornerback Nahshon Wright, the NFL’s takeaways leader last season, leave via free agency because they believed Stevenson was ready to retake his starting role. The pressure on the position has only ratcheted up during training camp because of the injuries to slot cornerback Kyler Gordon and safety Coby Bryant. Gordon, who hurt his calf, has no timeline to return. Bryant, who hurt his knee earlier this week, will miss at least two months. Were the season to start today, Jaylon Jones, the Bears’ third-string slot cornerback, would be the starter.</p><p>Stevenson, then, needs to become the least of the Bears’ concerns.</p><p>“Tyrique is on a contract year,” Jaylon Johnson said. “He’s got to prove himself.”</p>

entries.title: Illinois Attorney General, city of Chicago sue Pullman Innovations over overwhelming odors — years later
entries.summary: <p>The city of Chicago and the Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul are suing Pullman Innovations, according to a joint statement from the attorney general and mayor’s office.</p><p>According to the lawsuit, the smells coming from Pullman Innovations’ vegetable oil plant have forced schools nearby to cancel recess and homeowners to stay inside with their windows shut, among other issues.</p><p>The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency had referred the matter after the plant's owners "allowed excessive odors, caused illegal air pollution, constructed a boiler without a permit that could cause or contribute to air pollution, and violated certain conditions of the operating permit at its Chicago facility," the offices said.</p><p>In 2024, city inspectors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" target="_blank" ><u>corroborated the overbearing odor</u></a>. Pullman Innovations at 100th Street and Torrence Avenue was featured in a 2023 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/2/10/23592110/polluters-pullman-innovations-air-quality-pollution-violations" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times investigation</u></a> that found city citations were doing little to thwart polluters across Chicago.</p><p>“Residents in the community surrounding the Pullman Innovations facility should be able to enjoy their lives and homes without having to endure the foul odors coming from the company’s operations,” Raoul said in a statement. “The company needs to address the odor issues and air pollution and ensure that its operations comply with Illinois’ environmental laws.”</p><p>Pullman Innovations didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The complaints go back years, as do inquiries by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Chicago Department of Public Health.</p><p>City inspectors described the entrance of the facility as having a “very strong odor that could best be described as rotting fish/decay of flesh” that made them “not want to breathe and made us nauseous,” according to a fall 2024 city report.</p><p>Some residents previously told the Sun-Times they thought the issue would stop when A-F Acquisition LLC took over the plant in 2016. Its previous owner, Agri-Fine, was sued by then-Illinois Attorney General Lisa Madigan after receiving being cited for several of its own violations.</p><p>In December, around 2,400 households full of people who have lived near the plant since 2018 were sent notice of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/01/13/pullman-innovations-class-action-lawsuit-odor-smells-southeast-side-dutch-farms" target="_blank" ><u>class action lawsuit seeking an undetermined cash settlement</u></a> over the putrid smells.</p><p>“When entities fail to act on City compliance mandates, we will use every tool available to us to ensure our residents are not subjected to environmental degradation,” Mayor Brandon Johnson said in a statement issued Wednesday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/2/10/23592110/polluters-pullman-innovations-air-quality-pollution-violations" >Polluters like Southeast Side plant often get a pass on air-quality violations in Chicago, Sun-Times finds</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" >Putrid smells from South Side plant enrage neighbors</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/01/13/pullman-innovations-class-action-lawsuit-odor-smells-southeast-side-dutch-farms" >Southeast Side residents face Friday deadline for lawsuit over horrible smells</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Welch's new working group to address Springfield harassment doesn't go far enough, Rep. Kelly Cassidy says
entries.summary: <p>A new initiative announced Wednesday by embattled Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch does little more than pay “lip service” to addressing Springfield’s persistent culture of sexual harassment, according to an influential Chicago Democrat in Welch’s caucus.</p><p>During an apology tour with local media outlets in the wake of his office’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/31/harry-benton-report-legislative-inspector-general-speaker-chris-welch-sexual-harassment" target="_blank" ><u>delayed response</u></a> to allegations of sexual harassment by disgraced ex-state-Rep. Harry Benton, Welch said a new House Culture and Accountability working group will soon begin developing systemic changes.</p><p>But state Rep. Kelly Cassidy — who didn’t support Welch’s 2021 ascent as speaker over concerns about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/28/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-harry-benton-michael-j-madigan-sexual-harassment-inquiry" target="_blank" ><u>past allegations against Welch</u></a> — said she didn’t have confidence the group would be empowered to make a difference.</p><p>In a statement, Cassidy said she “asked a series of questions to ensure that the group would offer more than lip service or a PR stunt. My questions were not answered.”</p><p>“I believe a working group on this topic could be necessary and important,” Cassidy said. “But we have a responsibility to victims and survivors to ensure any such body is credible and effective, and I currently do not have confidence it will be. As such, I will not be participating at this time.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-520000" name="image-520000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1f81f09/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4121x2313+0+217/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2Fc1%2Fe807afd8c688549dca67aee4a9bf%2Fcassidy-kelly-0.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cdfa721/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4121x2313+0+217/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2Fc1%2Fe807afd8c688549dca67aee4a9bf%2Fcassidy-kelly-0.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bac694f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4121x2313+0+217/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2Fc1%2Fe807afd8c688549dca67aee4a9bf%2Fcassidy-kelly-0.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Kelly Cassidy speaks with reporters in 2018." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bac694f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4121x2313+0+217/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2Fc1%2Fe807afd8c688549dca67aee4a9bf%2Fcassidy-kelly-0.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/60f62af/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4121x2313+0+217/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2Fc1%2Fe807afd8c688549dca67aee4a9bf%2Fcassidy-kelly-0.jpeg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bac694f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4121x2313+0+217/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F79%2Fc1%2Fe807afd8c688549dca67aee4a9bf%2Fcassidy-kelly-0.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>State Rep. Kelly Cassidy said creating a new House Culture and Accountability working group doesn’t go far enough in addressing sexual harassment in the legislature.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Welch <a class="Link" href="https://wgntv.com/news/illinois-house-speaker-breaks-silence-on-ethics-controversy-full-interview/" target="_blank" ><u>told WGN-TV</u></a> the group led by state Rep. Dagmara Avelar, D-Bolingbrook, will meet for the first time next week “and their charge is to make some recommendations to us for legislation.”</p><p>It’s the most tangible response to the scandal yet from the three-term speaker, who acknowledged he failed to adequately address the initial allegation against Benton, but insisted his office was hamstrung because the victim did not want to file a formal complaint.</p><p>Welch also apologized for sending emojis that made the complainant uncomfortable in their social media interactions with Welch, resurrecting concerns about harassment in the Capitol and whether the speaker is adequately addressing the issue.</p><p>He made <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/04/pritzker-welch-benton-harassment" >his first public comments</a> five days after the release of a legislative inspector general’s report on Benton’s alleged misconduct, which showed Welch was aware of allegations against Benton but still put $1.4 million into his reelection campaign. Representatives for the speaker ignored repeated requests for comment from the Sun-Times.</p><p>“My office did its best,” Welch told WGN. “They followed their processes and procedures in place. But clearly, we failed this young woman and all women who are afraid to come forward. The system failed. We can do better.”</p><p>Welch said his former chief of staff “heard that something was going on” in Benton’s office in 2023, reached out to the woman and encouraged her to document her allegations that the representative made a series of troubling sexual comments.</p><p>Welch noted the state’s “biggest new tool” in the wake of the 2018 harassment scandal that preceded <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/2/20/18329507/velvet-hammer-mike-madigan-getting-nailed-by-more-and-more-fellow-democrats" target="_blank" ><u>ex-Speaker Michael Madigan’s downfall</u></a> was the legislative inspector general process, which the victim did not want to pursue.</p><p>“Even though she didn't want to go through a formal complaint process, we did do an informal investigation, and we still documented Rep. Benton because of the information that was brought forward,” Welch said. “And it was that information that we documented that allowed me to move swiftly when things came forward in 2026.”</p><p>Political committees controlled by Welch still backed the hotly contested 2024 reelection bid by Benton, who “was entitled to a constitutional right to due process,” Welch said.</p><p>“I had to support a member, and I supported a member. Obviously, today as we sit here, do I regret that? Certainly,” Welch said.</p><p>That changed early this year, when a lobbyist accused Benton of making lewd comments to her at a River North bar. Welch removed Benton from the Democratic caucus pending the investigation by the legislative inspector general. Ultimately, Welch called for Benton's resignation.</p><p>Benton, who has denied wrongdoing, stepped down last month.</p><p>As for sending heart-eye emojis in response to a complainant’s Instagram feed, Welch said he never thought it would make her feel uncomfortable until she shared details of the exchange with the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/07/17/state-rep-harry-benton-harassment-claims/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Tribune</u></a>.</p><p>“I sincerely want to apologize to her, because it was never my intent to make her or anyone feel uncomfortable,” Welch said. “I certainly have learned a lot from this situation, certainly have changed, already, my social media behavior.”</p><p>He also downplayed his invitation to the woman via an encrypted messaging site to meet at Gibson’s Bar in Oak Brook, “a place that I have a whole lot of meetings” at, Welch said. “But I understand the optics of that, and again, I'm going to apologize for making her feel uncomfortable.”</p><p>The speaker also denied his abrupt public statement <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/04/mayor-brandon-johnson-cps-budget-schools-funding-tif-surplus-springfield-state-funding" target="_blank" ><u>in support of supplemental state funding for Chicago Public Schools</u></a> — a long-shot in the cash-strapped Capitol — was made in an effort to shore up support for his speakership.</p><p>“That's what I've always done, but that fight isn't just for CPS,” Welch said. “That fight's for all schools.”</p>

entries.title: Cook County sees 10th heat-related death of 2026, further passing decade-old high
entries.summary: <p>A man died of heat-related reasons Tuesday just a block away from several hospitals, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>The 64-year-old man, whose name has yet to be released, died of cardiovascular disease complications and heat stress in the 1000 block of South Wood Street Tuesday around 6 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office. </p><p>His death in the 1000 block of South Wood Street makes for 10 deaths related to heat this year in Cook County, the highest number of deaths in a single year in more than a decade, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis</u></a> of data from the medical examiner’s office.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-780000" name="html-embed-module-780000"></a><div style="min-height:527px" id="datawrapper-vis-Swgb9"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Swgb9/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Swgb9"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Swgb9/full.png" alt="Ten people have died so far this year in Cook County from heat-related causes, the most in a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In 2019 and again in 2022, six people died from heat-related causes.</p><p>The others whose deaths have at least in part been attributed to the heat this year are Joseph Huff, 65; Robert Feldon, 77; Stephanie Rodriguez, 45; David Gonzalez, 44; Barbara Whigham, 71; Mike Rodriguez, 57; Daniel Machnikowski, 69; Victor Ferguson, 48; and David P. Sopys, 46.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-180000" name="html-embed-module-180000"></a><div style="min-height:849px" id="datawrapper-vis-YzdKE"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/YzdKE/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-YzdKE"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/YzdKE/full.png" alt="Heat-related causes have killed ten so far in Cook County (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago State prepares to make history as Division I football returns to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Players cycled through warm-ups, worked at individual position drills and scrimmaged under the watchful eyes of coaches and gathered media Wednesday at Chicago State University.</p><p>It was a lot like any other media day for a lot of Division I football programs. Except this was Chicago State University, and it's never had a football team before.</p><p>For senior safety Marlon Ayers Jr., the significance of the day stretched far beyond what happened between the lines.</p><p>"It was never really about football," Ayers said.</p><p>Indeed, Wednesday's open practice at the Emil and Patricia A. Jones Convocation Center was a milestone for both the university and the city. It also offered the first public glimpse of a program working to establish a culture built on accountability, resilience and community.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: MVP race is more like heavyweight fight between Pete Crow-Armstrong, Shohei Ohtani as Cubs sweep Dodgers
entries.summary: <p>There’s plenty of speed to go around between Pete Crow-Armstrong and Shohei Ohtani, a couple of baseball’s elite base-stealers.</p><p>But their race for the NL MVP is looking less like a race and more like a heavyweight fight.</p><p>The duo took turns delivering haymakers Wednesday, with each guy homering twice in a classic between the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and Dodgers, Crow-Armstrong setting himself up as very much a legitimate challenger to Ohtani, the once-in-forever two-way star who’s won four MVP awards in the last five years.</p><p>“Today showed that both of them are superstars,” Cubs lefty starter Shota Imanaga said, “especially Pete.</p><p>“Being able to play with him, be teammates with him, that’s such an honor. Once I’m done playing baseball, I’m going to talk about the fact that I got to play with such a great player.”</p><p>Ohtani started another season as the obvious favorite to win another MVP, just like his Dodgers started another season as the obvious favorites to win another World Series.</p><p>But the Cubs spent three days <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-dodgers-three-peat-world-series-favorites-tarik-skubal-dansby-swanson" >proving themselves challengers</a> to the Dodgers’ throne, playing high-quality, all-around baseball in a sweep of the back-to-back champs, finishing things off with a 7-6 win Wednesday.</p><p>And Crow-Armstrong, as he’s done all season, was right in the middle of everything. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" >That includes the MVP conversation</a> with the best baseball player on the planet.</p><p>Can Crow-Armstrong dethrone Ohtani? Can the Cubs dethrone the Dodgers?</p><p>“Simply put, just having your name in the same conversation as someone as profound as he feels, it’s awesome and it’s a nice nod,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I would feel much more accomplished taking [the Dodgers] down at some point.</p><p>“I want to see this [Cubs] group in October because I think it will be a dangerous, dangerous group in the playoffs.”</p><p>If Wednesday was a preview of what a Cubs-Dodgers series might look like in the postseason, fans are in for a treat.</p><p>Ohtani led off the game with a homer, only for Crow-Armstrong to answer with a homer in the bottom of the first inning. Crow-Armstrong followed with an RBI double and a home run launched off the right-field video board as the Cubs built a six-run lead.</p><p>Ohtani came up clutch, capping a five-run Dodgers eighth with a homer that shaved the Cubs’ lead to the minimum, only for Jacob Webb to shut the door with his second 1-2-3 ninth in as many days.</p><p>“You know it’s going to be tough to beat them. You know it’s not going to happen easily,” manager Craig Counsell said. “We’re playing good baseball. We played good baseball in all facets. To beat them three times, it’s not one or the other, it’s got to be everything.”</p><p>Ohtani is still doing things that have never been done before. While health concerns have limited him to only 14 starts this season, he’s been spectacular when on the mound, with a 1.79 ERA that ranks second in baseball among pitchers who have thrown at least 80 innings.</p><p>Meanwhile, Crow-Armstrong is making nightly highlight-reel plays in center field, showing he’s perhaps the best defender in the sport, coming into Wednesday the league-leader in both Outs Above Average (22) and Fielding Run Value (24).</p><p>As they both rack up best-in-baseball type offensive numbers, too, their impacts beyond the batter’s box could wind up the difference in who takes home the hardware at season’s end.</p><p>Looks like Crow-Armstrong – whose 7.5 fWAR led baseball entering Wednesday – is going to have to take his game to another place if he’s going to find an edge.</p><p>“If you guys want to talk about all this back and forth,” he said, “I really should get in the lab and start pitching. I really should.”</p><p>Who knows how the playoff bracket will line up, but an October rematch would be must-see TV, with Cubs vs. Dodgers – and Crow-Armstrong vs. Ohtani – looking like the game’s latest and greatest heavyweight fight.</p><p>Will it be “down goes Ohtani” in the MVP race? How about “down go the Dodgers” in the playoffs?</p><p>For three days in August, Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs made it look like they could be the ones to deliver a knockout punch.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Daniel Palencia nearing return from IL, but Cubs will be ‘flexible’ while Jacob Webb shines as go-to reliever
entries.summary: <p><b>Daniel Palencia</b> is nearing a return from the injured list.</p><p>But that doesn’t necessarily mean he’ll be stepping right back into his role as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ closer.</p><p>Righty <b>Jacob Webb</b> has been terrific as the team’s closer/go-to reliever in games’ biggest moments. He has a 2.49 ERA and has been on a roll lately, without a run allowed in his last 18 appearances, including back-to-back 1-2-3 ninths in wins over the juggernaut Dodgers on Tuesday and Wednesday.</p><p>But perhaps independent of Webb’s success, whether the fireballing Palencia is destined to retake his place in the ninth inning or not, the Cubs aren’t planning to hand the keys back to someone whose season has been limited to just a handful of games by two IL stays.</p><p>“Initially, when Daniel comes back, we certainly should be flexible with where he pitches and just get him into some appearances,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Wednesday. “If we get to a place where we’re getting a little bit more defined [with roles], great. If we don’t, great. But certainly, when he comes back, we’re going to be flexible.”</p><p>Palencia has logged only 16 2/3 innings, much of his summer wiped out by elbow inflammation that’s sidelined him since mid June.</p><p>Palencia’s return is near, though not exactly imminent. Counsell said Palencia will make more than one minor league rehab appearance before coming back.</p><p>But Webb has earned the right to keep getting the call in the most critical late-inning moments, while Palencia needs to get his feet back under him before getting the types of assignments he’s had in the past.</p><p>“[Palencia] just hasn’t pitched [much] this year,” Counsell said. “That’s probably my concern right now. We’ve got to get innings under his belt. We think the injury is behind him, but we’ve got to be careful, too, at the start here. We’ve got to get some innings under his belt, too.”</p><p><b>No ‘revenge game’</b></p><p><b>Kevin Gausman</b> getting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/02/dodgers-getting-tarik-skubal-only-makes-cubs-road-tougher" >traded from the Blue Jays to the Cubs</a> means the righty won’t get a crack at a “revenge game” Thursday, when the two teams clash in a makeup of a rained-out June contest.</p><p>Gausman pitched in one of the other games in that series and was scorched for seven runs by the Cubs.</p><p>Upon discovering he’d been dealt to the Cubs, his dreams of revenge were dashed.</p><p>Then another emotion: Would he have to face his former team?</p><p>That won’t happen, either, with his Cubs debut set for this weekend in Kansas City.</p><p>“I’ve kind of had this [makeup] game circled for a while, knowing it was going to be my ‘revenge game,’” he joked Wednesday. “At first, [after the trade], I thought I was maybe going to pitch against the Blue Jays. That was going to be a little strange.”</p><p><b>Stuck in second</b></p><p>The Cubs came into Wednesday with the best record in the NL since June 11, at 31-15, but made up next to no ground on the division-leading Brewers during that stretch, with the NL Central’s top team going a barely-worse 29-18.</p><p>Though the Cubs are rolling, should they be worried about catching the Brewers?</p><p>“That’s not going to help,” Counsell said. “We would like to make up ground, but worrying about it is not going to help me do it. We get an opportunity to play them. That’s when we can worry about it. Other than that, we’ve just got to do our thing.”</p><p>The Cubs and Brewers play each other seven times during a 10-day stretch starting Aug. 31.</p>

It blends storytelling with original songs co-written with Todd Almond. Annie Tippe directs. At 7:30 p.m. Aug. 6-7, 3 and 7:30 p.m. Aug. 8, 3 p.m. Aug. 9 at Steppenwolf Theatre, 1650 N. Halsted St. Tickets: $79-$125. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://steppenwolf.org" target="_blank" ><u>steppenwolf.org</u></a>.</li><li><b>Broadway in Chicago Summer Concert</b> features songs from “The Who’s Tommy,” “The Bodyguard,” “Disney’s The Lion King” and “Heathers: The Musical” all coming to Chicago in 2027. Additional performances include songs from “The Sound of Music,” “The Notebook,” “The Outsiders,” “Jekyll & Hyde,” “Mincemeat: A New Musical” and more. At 6:15 p.m. Aug. 10 at Pritzker Pavilion, 201 E. Randolph St. Admission is free. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://broadwayinchicago.com" target="_blank" ><u>broadwayinchicago.com</u></a>.</li></ul><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-070000" name="image-070000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/95ec76a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1200x673+0+563/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F99%2Fb2589af4414f9032d70a4f08c5ad%2Fwhat-are-you-going-to-do-actor-alex-edelman-photo-by-emilio-madrid.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7f48bd6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1200x673+0+563/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F99%2Fb2589af4414f9032d70a4f08c5ad%2Fwhat-are-you-going-to-do-actor-alex-edelman-photo-by-emilio-madrid.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/381439f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1200x673+0+563/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F99%2Fb2589af4414f9032d70a4f08c5ad%2Fwhat-are-you-going-to-do-actor-alex-edelman-photo-by-emilio-madrid.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="What Are You Going to Do - From Aug. 12-16 at Steppenwolf Theatre, 1650 N. Halsted St. Tickets: $54-$94. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://steppenwolf.org" target="_blank" ><u>steppenwolf.org</u></a>.</li><li>PrideArts presents Chicago playwright Matt Schutz’s <b>“Windows,”</b> a comedy about LGBT Gen Zers finding their ways through career and relationship challenges. Directed by Taylor Pasche. From Aug. 7-23 at Hoover-Leppen Theatre, Center on Halsted, 3656 N. Halsted St. Tickets: $35. entries.title: Naperville woman sentenced to 38 years for murdering fiancé
entries.summary: <p>A Naperville woman was sentenced to 38 years in prison this week for fatally shooting her husband during an argument in 2020, according to the DuPage County State’s Attorney’s office.</p><p>Rosa Lagrone, 40, was found guilty of first-degree murder in February, according to the office.</p><p>On the afternoon of Nov. 6, 2020, Lagrone and her fiancé, Darnell Manns, were arguing about him allegedly seeing another woman. During the argument in her home, in the first block of 25W Keswick Lane, she shot him in the arm, prosecutors said.</p><p>Lagrone then used Manns’ Facebook page to video chat the woman he was allegedly seeing as he lay on the ground bleeding, prosecutors said. He was taken to a nearby hospital and died of his injuries three days later.</p><p>“No number of years will bring Darnell back to those who loved him and those he loved,” said DuPage County State’s Attorney Bob Berlin in a statement. “Their grief will far outlast Ms. Lagrone’s sentence, and I wish them strength as they navigate their lives without the love, comfort and support once provided by Darnell.”</p>

entries.title: Man arrested toting Molotov cocktails accused of possibly targeting Orland Park mosque, police say
entries.summary: <p>A 31-year-old man arrested over the weekend allegedly toting more than half a dozen Molotov cocktails in his backpack was possibly planning to threaten an Orland Park mosque, police said. </p><p>It was about 2:55 a.m. Saturday when Mokena police officers spotted Hamed Alsaidi walking in the middle of 191st Street near LaGrange Road, Mokena Police Chief Brian Benton said, adding it was actually the second time officers encountered him in the space of a few hours. </p><p>But when officers stopped him that second time, Alsaidi, of the 5700 block of Circle Drive in Oak Lawn, gave them a false name, Benton said. </p><p>When officers learned of the bogus name, Alsaidi was taken into custody for walking in the roadway and giving officers a fake name and he was searched, a search that included the backpack he was wearing, the chief said. </p><p>Inside the backpack they found a blanket and seven or eight glass bottles of various sizes filled with what appeared to be alcohol, with cloth stuffed in them, according to Benton. </p><p>Also in the backpack officers found the word "mosque" scribbled on a scrap of paper. Also on the paper were a drawing and directions, according to Benton. </p><p>"We called our state fire marshal and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the FBI to assist in the investigation," Benton said. </p><p>Earlier that evening, officers had been called to a gas station at 187th and Wolf to look into a report of a suspicious person who behind the building, Benton said. "They asked him what he was doing and he said he was just looking for a place to sleep," Benton said.</p><p>Alsaidi said he wanted to go to a Quick Mart nearby, so officers gave him a lift and dropped him off there, Benton said. </p><p>"He didn't do anything wrong but they did keep an eye out the next few hours," Benton said.</p><p>Ultimately, the Will County state's attorney's office later approved charges of unlawful use of a weapon and obstructing a peace officer, both of which are felonies, Benton said. </p><p>In a<a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/search/top/?q=orland%20park%20police" target="_blank" > Facebook post,</a> Orland Park police said they learned the Mokena arrest possibly involved threats directed toward the Orland Park Prayer Center, a mosque at 16530 104th Ave. in Orland Park. </p><p>Since learning of the incident, the Orland Park Police Department has remained in close communication with the Mokena Police Department, federal law enforcement and security personnel at the Orland Park Prayer Center, according to the post. </p><p>A Will County judge on Sunday released Alsaidi on home monitoring. Alsaidi was expected back in court on Aug. 24, according to Benton.<br></p>

entries.title: Suburban 'backyard rodeos' feature steers being chased, knocked down and, at times, stripped of their tails
entries.summary: <p>A man on horseback in a corral rides feverishly alongside a fleeing steer while reaching for the animal’s tail, which he quickly but skillfully wraps around his right cowboy boot while maintaining a grip on the appendage.</p><p>As intended, the maneuver causes the steer to twist and tumble to the dirt.</p><p>The rider — part of a “backyard rodeo” in the far northwest suburbs last summer — gallops off, holding something grotesque in his hand: part of the steer’s tail, which was ripped free.</p><p>Called “degloving,” the injury is common at these types of events, according to local animal rights activists who have been trying to stop “steer tailing” in Illinois for years, saying it amounts to animal abuse that’s clearly illegal under state law, though not enforced nearly enough by local police and prosecutors.</p><p>An exception is in McHenry County, where three men were sentenced Wednesday to a year of conditional discharge, similar to probation, on animal cruelty charges stemming from last summer’s event in unincorporated Woodstock. Imposed by Judge Justin Hansen, the sentence included $250 fines and barred the men from "intentional contact" with animals, with some exceptions, during the term.</p><p>The men were prosecuted, at least in part, based on drone footage of the rodeo taken by the animal advocacy group SHARK, which stands for Showing Animals Respect and Kindness. The organization has documented similar events in far south suburban Will County and areas downstate, including Ogle County.</p><p>Court records say one of the men in McHenry County, Alfredo Magallanes, “participated in a rodeo steer-tailing event” at which he “knowingly pulled the tail of a live steer with sufficient force which caused a degloving injury that was captured on drone video.”</p><p>“The act caused pain and exposed the animal to further harm and infection, constituting cruel treatment of the steer, contrary” to state law.</p><p>A 24-year-old Marengo resident, Magallanes pleaded guilty, as did two other men similarly charged, records show.</p><p>Each apologized in court Wednesday and portrayed the tail injuries as unintentional, with their attorney Garrett Fisher telling Hansen: “These were all accidental events" in what's “a very physical and demanding sport” that "in no way rewards or encourages” harming animals.</p><p>Prosecutor Joe Creager responded: "To call this a sport or even a demanding sport is offensive to rodeo . . . this is punishing cows for sport."</p><p>A juvenile from Lockport was also initially cited, but that case was dropped.</p><p>A fifth person, 68-year-old Socorro Barrientos, already went on trial but a judge hasn’t yet rendered a decision, according to court records that say the defendant kicked “a steer in the head over 10 times” at the same event as the others “while it was on the ground and not posing a threat.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> </div><p>Chicagoan Jodie Wiederkehr, SHARK’s campaigns director, doesn’t believe steer-tailing and backyard rodeos are necessarily becoming more common in the region, but rather more attention is being paid to them because activists are highlighting the maltreatment that often occurs.</p><p>“The reason it’s going on is because there’s a lot of money being made,” Wiederkehr says, noting tickets to attend the private events can run $50 apiece and they are fashioned to be festive, with “dancing and drinking and having fun” in addition to the rodeo displays.</p><p>She says the treatment of steers amounts to torture, even when their tails aren’t torn away.</p><p>Another SHARK video from a backyard rodeo there shows a steer limping off with an apparent broken leg after being taken down by a rider on horseback.</p><p>Wiederkehr says the animals are sometimes poked or hit with sticks, shocked with cattle prods, worked until exhausted and even bitten on their tails by rodeo participants in an apparent attempt to stimulate the creatures.</p><p>“These animals are often left to suffer for hours without veterinary treatment or pain relief,” says Wiederkehr, who was instrumental in getting the City Council to vote in 2020 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2020/3/11/21175331/horse-drawn-carriages-ban-chicago-brendan-reilly-brian-hopkins" target="_blank" >to ban horse-drawn carriages in Chicago</a> over concerns about their well-being.</p><p>Illinois’ Humane Care for Animals Act says: “No person or owner may beat, cruelly treat, torment, starve, overwork or otherwise abuse any animal.”</p><p>Animal owners must provide "veterinary care when needed to prevent suffering.”</p><p>SHARK president Steve Hindi, who’s based in Kane County, said that too often authorities in Illinois don’t enforce the law, even in the face of clear evidence.</p><p>One argument Hindi’s group has heard: The statute doesn’t specifically ban steer tailing.</p><p>To which Hindi says: “There’s no law that” explicitly “says you can’t throw a puppy out a window,” but the anti-cruelty statute would clearly cover that.</p><p>“We shouldn’t need a new law,” he says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ae0000" name="image-ae0000"></a> <picture Rachel Ventura (D-Joliet) in the General Assembly last year to specifically ban steer tailing. The measure read in part: “No person may intentionally drag or pull any bovine by its tail by any means for the purpose of entertainment, sport, practice, or contest.”</p><p>Co-sponsored by state Sen. Li Arellano Jr. (R-Dixon), the bill failed to advance this year. Passing instead in the Illinois Senate was a non-binding resolution that frowned on steer tailing, saying “we discourage all acts of bovine tailing and its associated harms.”</p><p>There’s been some resistance to cracking down on steer tailing, called “coleadero” in Spanish, because of its place in Mexican rodeo culture dating back centuries.</p><p>Arellano says that doesn't change the fact that the “the injury rate is higher than almost any other rodeo event,” and he knows of no reputable U.S. rodeo organization that currently promotes steer tailing, whether Mexican-style events or the
